workload_suite.prompt_text: Explain the principle of cache locality in computer memory hierarchies, distinguishing between temporal and spatial locality.
Explain the principle of cache locality in computer memory hierarchies, distinguishing between temporal and spatial locality.

Explain the principle of cache locality in computer memory hierarchies, distinguishing between temporal and spatial locality. Discuss why modern processor architectures utilize multi-level hierarchical caches (L1, L2, and L3) to bridge the persistent performance gap between high-frequency arithmetic logic units and high-latency main system memory. Describe how cache lines are typically structured and transferred in 64-byte blocks, and analyze the computational consequences of sequential array traversal versus random pointer chasing in linked structures.

Analyze the operational intensity of transformer neural network inference across both the prefill and autoregressive decode phases. In the prefill phase, the entire prompt sequence is processed simultaneously, allowing matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM) that achieve high arithmetic intensity and saturate compute units (ALUs/tensor cores). In contrast, during the autoregressive decode phase, generation proceeds one token at a time, requiring matrix-vector operations (GEMV) where all model parameters must be read from memory for each single generated token. Discuss why the decode phase becomes severely memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. Explain the role of the key-value (KV) cache in storing previous token representations to avoid redundant quadratic computation, and how the KV-cache size scales with batch size, sequence length, number of attention layers, and hidden dimensions. Finally, contrast standard multi-head attention (MHA) with grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-query attention (MQA) in reducing memory bandwidth demands during decoding. Explain how KV-cache paging mechanisms like vLLM PageAttention mitigate external and internal memory fragmentation during multi-tenant serving, and why memory capacity often forms a hard upper ceiling on achievable batch concurrency before arithmetic execution units reach thermal or utilization limits. Examine how prompt caching enables recurrent system prompts to bypass the quadratic prefill computation entirely by reusing prefix KV states.

Analyze the operational intensity of transformer neural network inference across both the prefill and autoregressive decode phases. Discuss why the decode phase becomes severely memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. Explain the role of the key-value (KV) cache in storing previous token representations to avoid redundant quadratic computation, and how the KV-cache size scales with batch size, sequence length, number of attention layers, and hidden dimensions. Finally, contrast standard multi-head attention (MHA) with grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-query attention (MQA) in reducing memory bandwidth demands during decoding. Explain how KV-cache paging mechanisms like vLLM PageAttention mitigate external and internal memory fragmentation during multi-tenant serving, and why memory capacity often forms a hard upper ceiling on achievable batch concurrency before arithmetic execution units reach thermal or utilization limits. Examine how prompt caching enables recurrent system prompts to bypass the quadratic prefill computation entirely by reusing prefix KV states. In addition to single-node memory bandwidth bottlenecks, evaluate how distributed inference strategies alter throughput and latency scaling across clusters. Tensor parallelism partitions weight matrices across multiple accelerators within a high-bandwidth NVLink domain, requiring all-reduce communication at every transformer layer. Pipeline parallelism instead partitions layers sequentially across devices, introducing pipeline bubbles and communication at stage boundaries. Sequence parallelism further shards activation tensors to reduce per-device memory consumption for very long context lengths. Compare these parallelization paradigms against mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, where only a sparse subset of expert feed-forward networks is activated per token. Detail how all-to-all communication overhead across multi-node interconnects can degrade throughput if communication bandwidth is constrained, and why expert placement strategies are vital for maintaining high hardware utilization. Furthermore, consider the operational trade-offs of post-training quantization schemes. Weight-only quantization, such as INT4 or INT8 GPTQ and AWQ, reduces the total memory bandwidth required to load model parameters on each decoding iteration without increasing compute requirements. However, when batch sizes grow sufficiently large that matrix operations transition from memory-bound GEMV to compute-bound GEMM, weight-only dequantization overhead can introduce computational bottlenecks unless mixed-precision tensor cores natively support low-precision arithmetic. Analyze how activation quantization (e.g., FP8 or INT8 W8A8) addresses this limitation by accelerating both compute and memory transfer, and discuss the numerical stability challenges associated with dynamic activation outliers across deep attention layers. Finally, assess speculative decoding techniques where a smaller draft model generates candidate tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by the target model during a single forward pass. Discuss why acceptance rates vary based on prompt domain, draft model capacity, and temperature, and under what conditions speculative execution succeeds in breaking the traditional memory-bandwidth wall of autoregressive decoding.
